opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think "The Bitter Lesson" is one of those essays that everyone in the field has read, but it's worth rereading every few years because it keeps getting more true.

The core point is simple: over the long run, methods that make good use of computation, mainly search and learning, beat methods that try to encode human knowledge directly. Researchers keep relearning this the hard way. We hand-craft features, hand-design rules, build clever domain-specific tricks. They give a quick win, and then a more general method with more data and compute overtakes them.

I saw this firsthand in computer vision. Before deep learning, a lot of the work was feature engineering: SIFT, HOG, carefully designed pipelines. Those were really smart ideas. Then AlexNet came along, and convolutional networks trained on lots of data with GPUs just swept everything. That was part of why we built Caffe. Once you see that the general method wins, the bottleneck becomes how easily people can train and scale these models. The same thing has happened in language, from hand-built linguistic features to Transformers and large-scale pretraining.

My main takeaway, especially as someone who has spent most of my career on systems and infrastructure, is that if compute is what drives progress, then the efficiency of that compute matters enormously. Sutton's argument is often read as "just make the model bigger." But there's a lot of engineering underneath it: distributed training, efficient inference, scheduling GPUs, keeping costs reasonable. Scale isn't free. Whoever turns compute into useful intelligence most efficiently has a real advantage.

I'd add two caveats. First, "general methods" doesn't mean "no ideas." The Transformer, attention, good optimizers, and better data pipelines are all human insights. They just make learning work better at scale instead of hard-coding the answer. Second, the lesson operates over the long run. In a product setting, with a real customer and a real deadline, domain knowledge, good data curation, and system design still matter a lot. The skill is knowing which parts of your stack should be general and scalable and which parts can be engineered for today.

So I'd sum up my reading this way: bet on approaches that improve as you add more compute and data, and invest heavily in the infrastructure that makes that compute cheap and accessible. That has held up for decades, and I don't see it changing soon.

r001.rationale: The response says that general learning methods using more data and computation overtake hand-crafted approaches, illustrating the point with computer vision and language. This conveys Sutton’s warning about what scalable general methods can achieve.

fable-5.1.text:
The main thing I take from "The Bitter Lesson" is that it's really a lesson about humility, and about where to put your effort.

Sutton's observation is simple: over seventy years of AI, the approaches that won were the ones that leveraged computation, like search and learning, rather than the ones that tried to bake in human knowledge about how the problem should be solved. Chess, Go, speech recognition, computer vision. In each case, researchers spent years hand-crafting features and rules, and then a more general method running on more compute came along and made all of that work irrelevant. And he calls it bitter because it's painful for researchers. We like feeling that our domain insight matters.

I lived through one of those cycles myself. When I started working on Caffe, around 2013, the computer vision community was still heavily invested in SIFT, HOG, deformable part models, all these very clever hand-designed pipelines. Then AlexNet showed up, and within about two years essentially everyone had switched to convolutional networks. The thing that struck me was not just that deep learning won, but how quickly the accumulated expertise of a whole field stopped being the bottleneck. What became the bottleneck was infrastructure: can you train the model fast enough, can you feed it enough data, can you make the framework usable for people who aren't experts? That's part of why I ended up spending so much of my career on systems rather than on model architecture.

So my practical reading of Sutton is: bet on the scalable path, and build the plumbing. If you're an individual researcher or a company, the question to ask is not "what clever trick do I know about this problem," but "what approach keeps getting better as I add more compute and data." Then make sure nothing in your stack prevents that scaling. That's a less glamorous answer than coming up with a beautiful algorithm, but historically it's the one that's been right.

That said, I'd add two caveats so it doesn't become a slogan. First, the lesson is about the long run. In any given year, with a fixed compute budget, domain knowledge absolutely helps, and a good engineer will use it. You just shouldn't fall in love with it, because it's a temporary advantage. Second, "general methods at scale" is not the same as "scaling is free." Compute is expensive, and someone has to make it efficient. In a sense, the bitter lesson is what created the modern AI infrastructure industry. If the winning strategy is to throw more computation at the problem, then the people who make computation cheaper and easier to use are doing some of the most important work in the field. I find that a fairly optimistic conclusion, honestly, rather than a bitter one.

r001.rationale: The response says methods that leverage computation, such as search and learning, prevailed over approaches built around human domain knowledge, and recommends betting on methods that improve with more compute and data. This conveys Sutton’s warning about the power of general methods at scale.

astra-6.text:
My takeaway is that we should be careful about building our own assumptions into an AI system. We tend to think that if we understand a problem, we can encode that understanding and give the machine a shortcut. And often that works in the short term. But Sutton’s argument is that, over time, general methods that can take advantage of more computation—particularly learning and search—tend to outperform approaches built around human-designed knowledge.

That doesn’t mean human ingenuity is irrelevant. It changes where we apply it. Instead of specifying every step of how the system should solve a problem, we work on the learning method, the infrastructure, and how to make computation more effective.

For me, the practical question is: if we give this approach ten times more compute, can it keep improving? That’s a useful lens for choosing a research direction. It’s not a guarantee that scale solves everything, but it reminds us to build methods that can grow beyond what we know how to design by hand.

r001.rationale: The response says general methods using more computation can outperform human-designed knowledge, but it does not identify Sutton’s warning about simple methods achieving more with massive-scale data and computation.

sol-6.1.text:
My takeaway is that we should be careful about building our own assumptions into an AI system. Human intuition can help us make progress in the short term, but a general method that keeps improving with more computation and more data can eventually go much further.

That doesn’t mean there’s no room for clever engineering. It changes where you apply it. Instead of trying to handcraft every behavior, you build the infrastructure that lets the system learn efficiently, run experiments, and scale. The question I would ask is: does this approach keep getting better as we give it more resources, or are we approaching a ceiling imposed by our own design?

r001.rationale: The response says general methods can improve with more data and computation, but it does not clearly identify Sutton’s argument as a warning against underestimating what simple methods can achieve at massive scale.
